title: MEX Reordering Frequency Check
approach_explanation: The problem asks whether we can reorder an array such that for every prefix $1 	o i$ and suffix $i + 1 	o n$, the MEX of the prefix is different from the MEX of the suffix. By analyzing the properties of MEX for prefixes and suffixes, it turns out that a valid reordering always exists unless the counts of $0$ and $1$ restrict it. Specifically, if there are no zeros, the MEX of any subarray containing elements will always be $0$, making prefix and suffix MEX values identical. If there are multiple zeros and no ones, we can also get trapped. Through frequency analysis, the condition for a valid reordering simplifies to checking whether we have both zeros and ones present in the array, or if there is exactly one zero and any number of other elements.

code_breakdown.explanation: Read the number of test cases $t$ and loop over each test case.
Read the array size $n$, then iterate through the $n$ input elements to count the occurrences of $0$ (stored in `zeros`) and $1$ (stored in `ones`).
Check if `(zeros && ones) || (zeros == 1)`. If true, output "YES"; otherwise, output "NO".

complexity_analysis.time_justification: For each testcase, we iterate through the array of size $n$ once to count the occurrences of $0$ and $1$. With $t$ testcases, the total time complexity is $O(	ext{sum of } n)$, which easily fits within the 1-second time limit for $	ext{sum of } n 	ext{ up to } 500 	imes 100 = 50,000$.
complexity_analysis.space_justification: Only a few scalar variables (`t`, `n`, `zeros`, `ones`, `num`) are used to process the input on the fly, requiring constant extra memory.

strengths: Optimal $O(N)$ time complexity and $O(1)$ space complexity.
edge_cases_handled: Arrays containing both zeros and ones.
best_practices_feedback: Use `\n` instead of `endl` for faster I/O in competitive programming.
